items.item: Amortized cost is total cost of a sequence of n operations divided by n, so it is a worst-case guarantee over any sequence, not a bound on any single operation.
Amortization is not average-case analysis: no probability or input distribution is involved, only averaging over time within one sequence.
Amortized also differs from expected cost of randomized algorithms: the average is over operations in a sequence, not over random outcomes of one operation.
Amortization pays off when the only way to get an expensive operation is to set it up with many cheap ones, so per-operation worst case is too pessimistic.

items.item: An accounting argument is valid only if the credit balance never goes negative; this invariant must be proved, otherwise the proof breaks down.
Accounting (taxation) charges may overcharge some operations and the amortized cost of an operation is the charge assigned to it, with tight bounds from schedules that just barely stay in the black.

items.item: Binary counter by aggregate: bit B[i] flips every 2^i-th increment, so n increments from zero flip fewer than 2n bits total, i.e. O(1) amortized versus Theta(log n) worst case per increment.

items.item: Binary counter by accounting: charge $2 when a bit goes 0 to 1 (one pays the flip, one is stored on the bit to pay its later reset); each increment sets exactly one bit, so amortized cost is 2.
Both counter and array analyses assume the sequence starts from the initial (empty/zero) state; the potential must start at 0 and stay non-negative, else an initial seed must be added to the bound.
Multipop-style operations (MultiPull(k) removing k items) are O(1) amortized because each item can be removed only once after being added, so removals are charged to earlier pushes.
Amortized bounds are not unique: different accounting schemes can assign different costs to the same operations, with no general reason to prefer one.

items.item: The potential method is the accounting method with the bank as a function of data structure state: amortized cost = actual cost + change in potential; for the counter, potential = number of 1 bits equals the unspent taxes.
Amortization hides worst-case latency: a single operation can still be slow, and worst-case-per-operation guarantees (e.g. Ehrlich's Gray counter, O(1) worst case) are a strictly stronger property.

at.quote: turning amortized bounds into worst-case ones

items.item: The aggregate method fails for mixed operation sequences (e.g. increment and decrement) because the sequence is unknown; the method also breaks for naive counters, which cost Theta(k) per op alternating 2^k and 2^k-1.
Shrinking a resizing array needs hysteresis: halve only at 1/4 full, not 1/2, otherwise alternating push/pop at a boundary thrashes and loses the constant amortized bound.
